card.title: When light behaves like thin straight pencils
card.meaning: Geometrical optics is the model of light as thin directional lines called rays when openings are much larger than the wavelength.
card.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="32,90 215,34 215,146" class="s"/><line x1="115" y1="16" x2="115" y2="58" class="lk"/><line x1="115" y1="122" x2="115" y2="164" class="lk"/><line x1="215" y1="16" x2="215" y2="164" class="lk"/><line x1="32" y1="90" x2="215" y2="34" class="lk"/><line x1="32" y1="90" x2="215" y2="146" class="lk"/><line x1="32" y1="90" x2="215" y2="90" class="ik"/><path d="M 62 81 A 32 32 0 0 1 62 99" class="lk"/><circle cx="32" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><text x="18" y="94" class="t">P</text><text x="115" y="13" text-anchor="middle" class="t">A</text><text x="115" y="174" text-anchor="middle" class="t">B</text><text x="162" y="82" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Ray (λ→0)</text><text x="226" y="28" class="t">S</text><text x="226" y="158" class="t">S'</text></svg>
card.picture: Look at the sharp cone of rays from P through wide opening AB onto screen SS'.
card.example: Visible light has a tiny wavelength near 0.0005 cm, so ordinary lenses and mirrors are huge compared to it.
card.bridge: In the mathematical limit where wavelength λ goes to zero, diffraction disappears and light energy follows thin paths called rays.

card.title: Why denser media count as longer paths
card.meaning: Optical path length is the vacuum distance that light would travel in the same time it takes to cross a medium.
card.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="65" y="24" width="80" height="52" class="s ok"/><line x1="24" y1="50" x2="185" y2="50" class="lk"/><line x1="65" y1="84" x2="65" y2="142" class="gk"/><line x1="145" y1="84" x2="145" y2="112" class="gk"/><line x1="65" y1="130" x2="185" y2="130" class="ik"/><circle cx="65" cy="130" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="185" cy="130" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="105" y="42" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Glass (n = 1.5)</text><text x="105" y="68" text-anchor="middle" class="t">d = 2 cm</text><text x="125" y="118" text-anchor="middle" class="t">L_op = n d = 3 cm</text><text x="125" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Same travel time τ in vacuum</text></svg>
card.picture: Compare the 2 cm glass block (top) with the 3 cm vacuum path (bottom) that takes the exact same time.
card.example: In glass with refractive index n = 1.5, a physical thickness of 2 cm has an optical path length of 1.5 × 2 cm = 3 cm.
card.bridge: Because speed in a medium is c / n, the time for step ds is (n ds) / c, so integrating n ds gives the optical path length.

card.title: How light chooses its path
card.meaning: Fermat's principle says light travels along a path whose travel time is stationary compared with slightly different nearby paths.
card.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M 30 138 Q 115 32 230 42" class="gk"/><path d="M 30 138 Q 148 148 230 42" class="gk"/><path d="M 30 138 Q 130 92 230 42" class="lk"/><path d="M 56 116 A 34 34 0 0 1 63 134" class="lk"/><circle cx="30" cy="138" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="230" cy="42" r="4" class="f"/><text x="16" y="146" class="t">A</text><text x="236" y="46" class="t">B</text><text x="82" y="52" class="t">Trial path C'</text><text x="112" y="88" class="t">Actual ray C</text><text x="148" y="148" class="t">δ ∫ n ds = 0</text></svg>
card.picture: Look at the solid ray ACB between the two dashed trial paths where small shifts do not change travel time.
card.example: In uniform air, the straight line between A and B has the shortest optical path. Inside an elliptical mirror, every path from focus S₁ to focus S₂ has the exact same length.
card.bridge: Therefore the modern statement replaces 'least time' with 'stationary optical path length': δ ∫ n ds = 0, allowing a minimum, maximum, or constant value.

card.title: Why only rays close to the axis focus sharply
card.meaning: The paraxial approximation keeps only rays that make very small angles with the symmetry axis of a curved surface.
card.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="16" y1="105" x2="244" y2="105" class="lk"/><path d="M 132 24 Q 104 105 132 162" class="lk"/><line x1="118" y1="56" x2="118" y2="105" class="gk"/><polyline points="28,105 118,56 226,105" class="lk"/><path d="M 56 90 A 32 32 0 0 1 60 105" class="lk"/><path d="M 196 105 A 30 30 0 0 1 199 92" class="lk"/><circle cx="28" cy="105" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="118" cy="56" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="226" cy="105" r="4" class="f"/><text x="28" y="122" text-anchor="middle" class="t">O</text><text x="66" y="98" class="t">α₁</text><text x="126" y="84" class="t">h</text><text x="118" y="122" text-anchor="middle" class="t">P</text><text x="226" y="122" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I</text><text x="130" y="156" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Small α₁: sin α₁ ≈ tan α₁ ≈ h/x</text></svg>
card.picture: Look at the small angle arc α₁ near O where height h divided by distance x gives the angle in radians.
card.example: At an angle of 0.1 rad (about 5.7°), sin(0.1) = 0.0998 and tan(0.1) = 0.1003, so sin φ₁ ≈ tan φ₁ ≈ φ₁.
card.bridge: Under this small-angle rule, all paraxial rays from object point O take equal time and meet at a single image point I.

card.title: Rays that stay in one flat slice versus skew rays
card.meaning: Meridional rays stay inside the plane that contains the optical axis, whereas skew rays twist out of a single plane.
card.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="24,118 76,34 236,34 184,118" class="s ok"/><line x1="34" y1="76" x2="226" y2="76" class="lk"/><polyline points="52,76 128,48 204,76" class="ik"/><polyline points="64,108 134,58 196,144" class="gk"/><circle cx="52" cy="76" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="76" r="4" class="f"/><text x="46" y="94" class="t">C₁</text><text x="206" y="94" class="t">C₂</text><text x="134" y="24" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Meridional ray (in plane)</text><text x="148" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Skew ray (leaves plane)</text></svg>
card.picture: Look at the solid meridional ray inside the flat axial slice, while the dashed skew ray leaves the slice in 3D.
card.example: Every ray starting from an object point on the optical axis is automatically a meridional ray.
card.bridge: When a system has two spherical surfaces, the line joining their centers C₁ and C₂ defines the optical axis.

card.title: Two spherical surfaces pressed close together
card.meaning: A thin lens is a transparent medium bounded by two spherical surfaces whose thickness is negligible compared to all other distances.
card.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="12" y1="96" x2="248" y2="96" class="lk"/><path d="M 118 26 Q 104 96 118 164 Q 132 96 118 26 Z" class="s ok"/><polyline points="26,96 118,46 218,96" class="lk"/><path d="M 50 83 A 28 28 0 0 1 54 96" class="lk"/><path d="M 192 96 A 26 26 0 0 1 195 84" class="lk"/><circle cx="26" cy="96" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="118" cy="96" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="218" cy="96" r="4" class="f"/><text x="26" y="114" text-anchor="middle" class="t">O</text><text x="118" y="18" text-anchor="middle" class="t">t ≪ |u|, |v|</text><text x="110" y="114" text-anchor="end" class="t">P</text><text x="218" y="114" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I</text><text x="72" y="138" text-anchor="middle" class="t">u (from P)</text><text x="168" y="138" text-anchor="middle" class="t">v (from P)</text></svg>
card.picture: Look at the thin lens at P: thickness t is so small that both u and v are measured from P.
card.example: Because thickness t is tiny, we measure object distance u and image distance v from one shared center P.
card.bridge: The first surface forms an intermediate image Q at v', which immediately acts as the object for the second surface to form final image I at v.

card.title: The two special focal points of any lens
card.meaning: The first principal focus F₁ turns rays from a point into parallel rays, while the second principal focus F₂ collects incoming parallel rays to a point.
card.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="12" y1="90" x2="248" y2="90" class="lk"/><path d="M 130 20 Q 116 90 130 160 Q 144 90 130 20 Z" class="s ok"/><polyline points="56,90 130,136 238,136" class="lk"/><polyline points="22,44 130,44 204,90" class="ik"/><circle cx="56" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="130" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><text x="56" y="78" text-anchor="middle" class="t">F₁</text><text x="122" y="106" text-anchor="end" class="t">P</text><text x="204" y="108" text-anchor="middle" class="t">F₂</text><text x="80" y="34" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Ray 2 (parallel → F₂)</text><text x="184" y="154" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Ray 1 (F₁ → parallel)</text><text x="92" y="122" text-anchor="middle" class="t">f₁ < 0</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" class="t">f₂ > 0</text></svg>
card.picture: Look at Ray 1 from F₁ emerging parallel, and parallel Ray 2 meeting the axis at F₂.
card.example: For a converging lens of focal length 20 cm in air, F₁ sits at f₁ = -20 cm (left) and F₂ sits at f₂ = +20 cm (right).
card.bridge: Setting v = ∞ gives u = f₁ (first focal length), and setting u = -∞ gives v = f₂ (second focal length).

card.title: How tall and which way up the image is
card.meaning: Lateral magnification compares the height of the image to the height of the object, including a sign for orientation.
card.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="14" y1="90" x2="246" y2="90" class="lk"/><path d="M 120 22 Q 108 90 120 158 Q 132 90 120 22 Z" class="s ok"/><line x1="38" y1="90" x2="38" y2="38" class="ik"/><line x1="216" y1="90" x2="216" y2="148" class="ik"/><line x1="38" y1="38" x2="216" y2="148" class="lk"/><path d="M 96 75 A 28 28 0 0 0 92 90" class="lk"/><path d="M 148 90 A 28 28 0 0 1 144 105" class="lk"/><circle cx="120" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><text x="24" y="66" class="t">y</text><text x="38" y="106" text-anchor="middle" class="t">O</text><text x="82" y="84" class="t">θ</text><text x="152" y="104" class="t">θ</text><text x="112" y="108" text-anchor="end" class="t">P</text><text x="216" y="82" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I</text><text x="228" y="130" class="t">y'</text><text x="78" y="136" text-anchor="middle" class="t">u < 0</text><text x="170" y="60" text-anchor="middle" class="t">v > 0 (m = v/u)</text></svg>
card.picture: Look at the equal angle arcs θ at lens center P: similar right triangles give m = y'/y = v/u.
card.example: A positive magnification (m > 0) means an erect image; a negative magnification (m < 0) means an inverted image.
card.bridge: For a thin lens in one medium, similar triangles through pole P give m = y' / y = v / u = -f₁ / x₁ = -x₂ / f₂.
